newsitem.title: ITALY: Glickman, Fischler avoid waves over grain policy.
newsitem.headline: Glickman, Fischler avoid waves over grain policy.

text.p: U.S. and European Union farm chiefs steered clear of recent controversy over grain export subsidies at a meeting in Rome on Thursday but focused instead on a tough drive towards mutual veterinary standards, officials said.

U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, joined by their aides, talked over dinner at Fischler's hotel for slightly over two hours on the sidelines of a five-day U.N. food summit.
"It was excellent -- the conversation, the meal, and my host was very hospitable," Glickman told Reuters after the dinner of pasta, fish and sorbet. He declined to say what was discussed.

Fischler said it was a valuable and constructive session but did not involve formal negotiation. Asked whether Glickman had brought up recent U.S. criticisms of EU wheat export subsidies, he said the issue had not entered the discussion.
"You must know that there is no reason for that because we reduced the refunds today," he told Reuters, referring to a weekly auction at which the EU granted less aid than before.
U.S. officials did not immediately comment on the issue, which has often caused trade clashes in the past.
Glickman said on Wednesday he had not ruled out restoring U.S. subsidies but indicated market conditions were improving.
An Australian cabinet minister said in Rome on Thursday he regretted the EU's decision to restore refunds in September and urged Brussels and Washington not to repeat a 1980s subsidy war.
Officials from both sides said the dinner talk instead dwelled on new, and highly technical, potential disputes over so-called veterinary and phytosanitary equivalency rules.
EU officials said last month that progress was being made towards agreeing a common set of rules, but many details had to be worked out to meet an end-year deadline.

The agreement, which involves mutual recognition of animal and plant health standards, covers trade in live animals, fresh and processed meat, pet food, plants and plant products worth up to $5.0 billion annually.
Among the problems in negotiations have been that Brussels wants Washington to cut a deal with the EU as a whole, not with individual states.
Washington is concerned about the extension of national standards into common EU standards, especially in the sensitive livestock trade.

EU officials said Glickman and Fischler also touched on U.S. concerns over access for genetically engineered foods into Europe, where environmentalists are waging a highly publicised campaign against U.S.-developed products.
Fischler said Glickman had raised the issue and that he had replied that the EU hoped to decide the way forward in mid-December.
The European Commission, aware of consumer unease in the wake of the scare over mad cow disease, said on Wednesday it would review the way the EU approves gene-modified products.
Commission President Jacques Santer made the pledge during the EU executive's weekly meeting, after talks on approval procedures for Ciba-Geigy AG's gene-modified maize, the Commission said.
The EU has already approved several gene-modified products including U.S. chemical company Monsanto Co's modified soybeans.
Glickman was himself caught on the hop by the "gene bean" campaign on Wednesday when three protestors stripped naked in front of him and hijacked the start of a Rome news conference.
